newsitem.title: USA: Rescuers start shoring up New Orleans Riverwalk.
newsitem.headline: Rescuers start shoring up New Orleans Riverwalk.

text.p: Rescuers began shoring up unstable sections of the New Orleans Riverwalk on Tuesday as a formal hearing looked into what caused a giant freighter to smash into the tourist attraction.

Rescue teams continued to search for possible victims in the rubble of the upscale shopping centre and a hotel wing that were badly damaged on Saturday when the 735-foot (224-metre) Bright Field lost power and crashed into the Poydras Street Wharf near the city's French Quarter.
Although 116 people were injured, only three remained in a hospital on Tuesday and no deaths were confirmed, officials said, calling the absence of fatalities "a Christmas miracle."
A fire department spokesman said crews began on Tuesday to stabilise sections of the building that have been too treacherous to search.

"It's just been too risky to put anybody in there," he said. Divers have been unable to search for victims under the crumbled concrete wharf because of hazards posed by the unstable rubble above, he said.

The Coast Guard's Marine Board of Investigation was scheduled to conduct joint hearings with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and the Republic of Liberia. Although owned by a Hong Kong company, the Bright Field was registered in Liberia.

Investigators trying to determine the cause of the accident will focus initially on the mechanics of the ship, whether the crew operated the systems properly, and whether language barriers between the Chinese crew and American river pilot affected responses, the Coast Guard said.

One Riverwalk shop owner, Gary Thomas, said little attention was paid to the Bright Field's marine emergency siren initially because cruise ships docking in the area sound similar blasts every Saturday during abandon-ship drills for new passengers.
"We hear that same alarm every Saturday," he said. "We've kind of become immune to that signal."
He called the Coast Guard to urge new controls on how and when cruise ships can test their emergency horns.

NTSB investigator John Hammerschmidt said the freighter, with a cargo of 64,000 short tonnes of corn, rammed into the wharf after its oil pump lost pressure and the pilot was unable to steer the ship.
He said a backup oil pump and automatic control system came on as they were supposed to, but the control system reduced the engine's speed, cutting the ship's manuverability.

River pilot Ted Davisson, who was at the ship's helm, used what little control he had to avoid two docked cruise ships with 1,700 passengers and a riverboat casino loaded with 800 gamblers, saving many lives, officials said.
